questions.question: What is Amazon EC2?
questions.answer: Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is an IaaS service that allows you to create and manage virtual servers (instances) in the AWS cloud. You select the OS, hardware specs, and configuration — AWS manages the physical infrastructure underneath.

questions.question: What is an AMI and what does it contain?
questions.answer: An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is a software configuration template used to launch EC2 instances. It contains the operating system, libraries, utilities, and optionally pre-installed applications. AWS provides ready-made Quick Start AMIs; you can also create custom AMIs.

questions.question: What is an EC2 instance type and what does it control?
questions.answer: An instance type defines the hardware configuration of your EC2 instance — specifically the number of virtual CPUs (vCPUs), RAM, and associated storage options. For example, t2.micro has 1 vCPU and 1 GB RAM.

questions.question: What are the five EC2 instance type families?
questions.answer: General Purpose (balanced CPU/RAM — all workloads), Compute Optimized (high CPU — video encoding, HPC), Memory Optimized (high RAM — databases, caching), Storage Optimized (high disk I/O — big data, Hadoop), and Accelerated Computing (GPU — machine learning, graphics).

questions.question: How does EC2 key pair authentication work?
questions.answer: When you create a key pair, AWS generates two cryptographically linked files: the public key is automatically stored on the EC2 instance, and the private key is downloaded to your laptop. When you SSH, you provide your private key. EC2 matches it against the stored public key. If they match, access is granted — no password needed.

questions.question: What is a Security Group in EC2?
questions.answer: A Security Group is a virtual stateful firewall that controls inbound and outbound network traffic to/from your EC2 instance. You define rules specifying which protocol (SSH, HTTP, etc.), port (22, 80, etc.), and source IP is allowed. Stateful means approved inbound traffic automatically allows the return outbound response.

questions.question: What is EBS and what is its default size for a new EC2 instance?
questions.answer: EBS (Elastic Block Storage) is the virtual hard drive attached to your EC2 instance. It stores the OS and application files. The default EBS volume size when launching a new instance is 8 GB. You can increase EBS size at any time.

questions.question: What is the default username for Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, and Windows EC2 instances?
questions.answer: Amazon Linux: ec2-user. Ubuntu: ubuntu. Windows Server: Administrator. Using the wrong username is one of the most common SSH connection errors.

questions.question: What is SSH and what port does it use?
questions.answer: SSH (Secure Shell) is a network protocol for securely logging into and controlling a remote computer over an encrypted connection. It uses port 22 by default. For Linux EC2 instances, SSH is the standard connection method.

questions.question: What is the difference between stopping and terminating an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: Stopping pauses the instance — compute billing stops, EBS is preserved, and you can restart later. Terminating permanently deletes the instance and its root EBS volume (by default). Termination cannot be undone. You stop paying compute when stopped, but EBS storage charges continue.

questions.question: Describe a time you launched a virtual server and what you configured.
questions.answer: (Situation) I needed to deploy a web project for a class assignment. (Task) Set up a cloud server capable of serving a website. (Action) I logged into AWS, selected the Mumbai region, launched an EC2 instance using the Amazon Linux 2023 AMI and t2.micro instance type, created a key pair, configured a Security Group to allow SSH (22) and HTTP (80), SSHed in using my private key, installed Apache httpd, and deployed my HTML files to /var/www/html/. (Result) The website was publicly accessible via the EC2 public IP in under 30 minutes.

questions.question: A colleague says their EC2 instance is running but they can't SSH into it. How would you troubleshoot this?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 running but SSH failing. (Task) Identify the cause and restore access. (Action) First, check the Security Group inbound rules — is SSH (port 22) open from the user's IP? Second, verify the correct username is being used (ec2-user for Amazon Linux). Third, confirm the correct private key file is specified. Fourth, check whether the public IP has changed (stop/start changes IPs). Fifth, ensure the .pem file exists in the current working directory. (Result) In most cases, missing port 22 rule or wrong username is the cause.

questions.question: Your application needs 16 GB RAM for in-memory data processing. Which instance type family would you choose and why?
questions.answer: (Situation) Application with high RAM requirement for in-memory processing. (Task) Select the right instance family. (Action) Memory Optimized instances (r-family, e.g., r5.large or r5.xlarge) are designed specifically for high RAM workloads — databases, caching layers, in-memory analytics. They provide a much higher RAM-to-vCPU ratio than general purpose instances. (Result) This ensures the application has sufficient memory without paying for unnecessary CPU capacity.

questions.question: You need to increase the CPU of a running EC2 instance from 2 vCPU to 8 vCPU. Walk me through the process.
questions.answer: (Situation) Existing EC2 instance needs more compute power. (Task) Upgrade the instance type with minimal disruption. (Action) Stop the instance (not terminate). Go to EC2 console → select the instance → Actions → Instance Settings → Change Instance Type → select new type (e.g., t3.2xlarge or m5.2xlarge). Start the instance. (Result) The instance comes back up with the new CPU/RAM configuration. All EBS data is intact. The public IP may change — note the new one.

questions.question: How would you deploy a static website on an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to host a static HTML website on EC2. (Task) Set up a web server and deploy files. (Action) Launch EC2 (Amazon Linux, t2.micro), open port 80 in Security Group, SSH in, run 'sudo yum install httpd -y', start the service with 'sudo systemctl start httpd', copy HTML files to /var/www/html/, then access via the public IP in a browser using http://. (Result) Website is publicly accessible to anyone on the internet.

questions.question: A developer accidentally stored their EC2 private key on GitHub. What should they do?
questions.answer: (Situation) Private key exposed on a public repository. (Task) Immediately secure the EC2 instance. (Action) 1. Create a new key pair immediately. 2. Add the new public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the EC2 instance (access using the old key if still available, or use AWS Session Manager). 3. Remove the old public key from authorized_keys. 4. Delete the old key pair from AWS console. 5. Revoke the exposed .pem file and remove it from GitHub history. (Result) Instance is secured with a new key; old key can no longer be used.

questions.question: Explain the complete request flow when a user accesses a website hosted on EC2.
questions.answer: (Situation) End user types the EC2 public IP in their browser. (Task) Trace the full journey of the request. (Action) Browser sends HTTP GET request to EC2's public IP on port 80 → Internet routes the request to AWS → Security Group checks inbound rules: is port 80 allowed? Yes → Request reaches the HTTPD (Apache) service listening on port 80 inside EC2 → Apache reads the requested file from /var/www/html/ on EBS → Returns the HTML response → Security Group (stateful) allows the response outbound → Browser renders the page. (Result) User sees the website.

questions.question: What is the difference between an AMI and a snapshot in EC2?
questions.answer: An AMI is a complete machine image used to launch new instances — it includes the OS, configuration, and can reference EBS snapshots. A snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS volume stored in S3. You can create a custom AMI from a running instance (which creates underlying snapshots). AMIs are used to launch instances; snapshots are used for backup and recovery.

questions.question: Why would you use a private IP instead of a public IP for communication between two EC2 instances?
questions.answer: Private IP communication stays entirely within the AWS internal network — it's faster (no internet routing), more secure (no public internet exposure), and free of data transfer costs. Public IP communication goes out to the internet and back, which is slower and incurs data transfer charges. Best practice: use private IPs for internal AWS traffic.

questions.question: You notice SSH connections to an EC2 instance are being attempted by unknown IPs thousands of times per hour. What would you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 SSH brute-force attack in progress. (Task) Secure the instance without losing access. (Action) 1. Update the Security Group inbound SSH rule to allow only your specific IP (/32 CIDR). 2. Consider disabling password authentication (already off by default). 3. Enable AWS CloudTrail and GuardDuty to monitor future unauthorized access attempts. 4. Review instance logs for any successful unauthorized logins. 5. Optionally, change to a non-standard SSH port. (Result) Attack surface significantly reduced; legitimate access preserved.

questions.question: Design a highly available web architecture using EC2 across multiple Availability Zones.
questions.answer: Deploy EC2 instances in at least two Availability Zones (e.g., ap-south-1a and ap-south-1b) with identical configurations using the same AMI. Place them behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) which distributes incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic across all healthy instances. Use Auto Scaling Groups to automatically add/remove instances based on traffic. Store shared data in RDS (Multi-AZ) or S3 rather than on individual EC2 EBS volumes. This ensures if one AZ fails, the other continues serving traffic with zero downtime.

questions.question: When would you choose Reserved Instances over On-Demand EC2 instances?
questions.answer: Reserved Instances are ideal when you have predictable, steady-state workloads that will run continuously for 1 or 3 years — like always-on production web servers or databases. They offer up to 72% cost savings vs On-Demand. On-Demand is better for unpredictable or short-term workloads. A hybrid approach is common: Reserve baseline capacity, use On-Demand or Spot for spikes.

questions.question: Explain the concept of EC2 User Data and how it can be used to automate instance configuration.
questions.answer: EC2 User Data is a script (Bash or PowerShell) you can provide at launch time that runs automatically when the instance first starts. It's used to bootstrap instances — installing software, pulling code from Git, starting services — without manual SSH intervention. For example, a User Data script could install Apache, clone a Git repo, and start the web server automatically on launch. This is foundational for auto-scaling and infrastructure automation.

questions.question: What is the difference between EC2 instance store and EBS? When would you use each?
questions.answer: EBS is a persistent, network-attached block storage volume — data survives instance stop/start/reboot. Instance store is temporary, physically attached storage on the host machine — data is lost if the instance stops, terminates, or the underlying hardware fails. Use EBS for anything you need to keep (OS, application data, databases). Use instance store only for temporary data: caches, buffers, scratch space where performance matters more than durability.

questions.question: How does EC2 Spot Instances work and what types of workloads benefit most from them?
questions.answer: EC2 Spot Instances let you bid for unused AWS capacity at up to 90% discount vs On-Demand. AWS can reclaim your Spot instance with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. Ideal for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads: big data processing (Hadoop/Spark jobs), batch processing, CI/CD build pipelines, ML training jobs, and video rendering — workloads that can be interrupted and restarted. Not suitable for databases, web servers, or any stateful application that needs continuous availability.
